title: Mastery Challenge: Logic & Critical Thinking
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Logic & Critical Thinking Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: One question per chapter: arguments, deduction, fallacies, evidence, causes, traps, science, persuasion, sources and decisions. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Logic & Critical Thinking Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from what an argument is to how to decide and think clearly. Level 1 asked whether dark windows really mean a café is closed; now see how far that one question reaches. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Logic & Critical Thinking: mastered
learned: How to take any argument apart, and test it for a valid form and true premises.
How classic fallacies dodge or distort the point, and why a fallacy never proves its conclusion false.
How to weigh evidence and causes: who is missing from the picture, and what hidden factor could fake a link.
How to catch your own reasoning traps, and test ideas the way science does: ask what would prove them wrong.
How to see past framing, weigh a source's interests fairly, and decide by what was known at the time.

questions.prompt: "The shop is shut, so it must be a holiday." Which unstated premise would make this work?

options.label: Holidays are good for business
options.rationale: That doesn't link shut to holiday.

options.label: The shop shuts only on holidays
Everyone likes a holiday
options.rationale: A taste claim does not help the argument.

options.label: Shops should open every day
options.rationale: A value judgment doesn't connect the claims.

questions.explanation: Ask what else must be true for the conclusion to follow: the shop shuts only on holidays.

questions.prompt: "All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly." What is wrong with this argument?

options.label: It's invalid: the conclusion doesn't follow
options.rationale: The form is airtight: if both premises were true, so would the conclusion be.

options.label: It's circular: it assumes what it proves
options.rationale: The conclusion is not simply restated in a premise.

options.label: It's valid but unsound: a premise is false
Nothing: a valid argument must be true
options.rationale: Only if its premises are true as well. That is soundness.

questions.explanation: The form is valid, but "all birds can fly" is false. Sound means valid plus true premises.

questions.prompt: "Don't take Omar's advice on fixing the bike. He failed science at school." Why is this a weak reply?

options.label: It restates Omar's advice as something sillier
options.rationale: That would be a straw man; his advice isn't restated at all.

options.label: It assumes its own conclusion
options.rationale: Nothing circular here; it rests on his grades.

options.label: It offers only two choices
options.rationale: No either/or is offered.

options.label: It aims at Omar, not at his reasons

questions.explanation: That's an ad hominem. Omar's advice can be checked on its own reasons; his old grades don't bear on it.

questions.prompt: A podcast interviews ten people who quit their jobs to start a business and got rich. It concludes quitting is a smart move. What is the main flaw?

options.label: It never hears from quitters who failed
Ten interviews are far too many to judge
options.rationale: More cases would help, not hurt; the problem is which cases.

options.label: It relies on experts outside their field
options.rationale: No experts are quoted; the gap is who is missing.

options.label: Stories about money can never be evidence
options.rationale: They can be; these ones passed through a filter first.

questions.explanation: Survivorship bias: only those who made it through the filter are in the picture. Ask who never made it into the picture.

questions.prompt: Towns with more ice rinks report more winter coughs. Which explanation should you check first?

options.label: The ice rinks are spreading the coughs
options.rationale: Possible, but the link alone does not show it.

options.label: Coughs lead towns to build more rinks
options.rationale: That reverses the cause, and nothing suggests it.

options.label: It's a coincidence with no link at all
options.rationale: There is an obvious third factor to check first.

options.label: Colder towns get more of both

questions.explanation: A cold climate brings rinks and coughs alike. Like hot weather behind ice cream and sunscreen, it is a confounder.

questions.prompt: A temple wall shows portraits of sailors who prayed and survived. Which habit best counters the trap behind treating it as proof?

options.label: Collect more portraits of the survivors
options.rationale: More hits don't answer the missing misses.

options.label: Look for sailors who prayed and drowned
Trust the view that most sailors hold
options.rationale: Popularity is not evidence.

options.label: Ask the priests how sure they feel
options.rationale: Confidence is not evidence either.

questions.explanation: Confirmation bias counts only the hits. Bacon's counter: seek the negative instance, the case that could prove you wrong.

questions.prompt: A fortune cookie says, "Something in your life will change soon." Why would Popper say this is not a scientific claim?

options.label: No possible outcome could show it is wrong
It has not yet been tested in a science lab
options.rationale: Untested is not the problem; untestable is.

options.label: It was written by a cookie company
options.rationale: Who wrote it doesn't decide whether it could fail.

options.label: It makes too bold a prediction
options.rationale: The opposite: it risks nothing at all.

questions.explanation: A scientific claim must stick its neck out. A claim that fits every outcome makes no real prediction.

questions.prompt: One yogurt says "90% fat-free." An identical yogurt says "10% fat." What does the idea of framing tell you?

options.label: The fat-free one has less fat in it
options.rationale: 90% fat-free means 10% fat: the same amount.

options.label: One of the two labels must be false
options.rationale: Each is true exactly when the other is.

options.label: They make one claim, framed two ways
The "10% fat" label uses weasel words
options.rationale: It is precise and checkable.

questions.explanation: The facts are equal; only the spotlight moved. A gain frame usually feels better, but it cannot change what is true.

questions.prompt: A study praising a new running shoe was paid for by the shoe's maker. What is the soundest response?

options.label: Throw it out, since the maker benefits
options.rationale: Dismissing it for that alone is an attack on the person.

options.label: Accept it, since it was published
options.rationale: A conflict is a real risk worth a closer look.

options.label: Ignore the funding; it never matters
options.rationale: Funding may sway judgment, which is why it is disclosed.

options.label: Check what the study measured, and how

questions.explanation: A conflict of interest is a risk, not a verdict. Rejecting a claim just because of who benefits is Level 22's ad hominem in new clothes.

questions.prompt: You spot a fallacy in a friend's argument that the café is open. What does that tell you about whether it's open?

options.label: That the café must be closed
options.rationale: That's the fallacy fallacy.

options.label: Nothing yet: check the café itself
That it's open after all
options.rationale: A fallacy tells you nothing either way about the claim.

options.label: That your friend can't be trusted on it
options.rationale: That's an attack on the arguer, not the claim.

questions.explanation: A fallacy is a flaw in the argument, not a verdict on its conclusion. Reject the argument, then check the claim on its own.
